621.event_title: Ronald Reagan jokes with his surgeons after being shot
621.event: On 30 March 1981 President Ronald Reagan was shot outside a Washington hotel; a bullet struck his left lung near his heart and he was rushed to George Washington University Hospital. According to accounts from people who were there, he lifted his oxygen mask moments before surgery and joked to the doctors that he hoped they were all Republicans, and one surgeon replied that today they all were. Reagan recovered and returned to the White House less than four weeks later.
621.explanation: A light-hearted remark at a moment of real danger steadied the people around him, and the Reagan Foundation has since presented it as a defining example of his calm and optimism.
621.tie_back: The kural advises meeting trouble with a smile because nothing overpowers sorrow so well, and Reagan's joke on the way into surgery is a vivid example of cheerful calm pressing back against a grave crisis.
621._accuracy_note: Very close to a dramatisation of smiling in the face of trouble; the exact wording of the joke varies slightly between accounts, so it is given here in prose.

622.event_title: Pombal directs the relief and rebuilding of Lisbon after the 1755 earthquake
622.event: On the morning of 1 November 1755 a series of earthquakes, followed by a tsunami and fires lasting about six days, devastated Lisbon and killed an estimated 60,000 people in the city. The king's chief minister, Sebastiao de Carvalho, later Marquis of Pombal, organised the aid and reconstruction effort. Rebuilding of the downtown began in 1756 on a new orthogonal street plan drawn up by Manuel da Maia and carried out by the military engineers Eugenio dos Santos and Carlos Mardel, with earthquake-resistant and fire-resistant buildings.
622.explanation: Instead of being overwhelmed by one of the worst disasters in European history, the government turned to orderly relief and a rational plan, and the rebuilt Baixa district still stands as a model of planned recovery.
622.tie_back: The kural says even a flood-like sorrow perishes once a wise person turns a steady mind upon it, and Lisbon's catastrophe was met by deliberate planning that turned ruin into a new city.
622._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of a steady mind mastering a vast calamity, though the response was a government effort rather than one individual's inner resolve, and Pombal's rule was also autocratic.

623.event_title: Karoly Takacs wins Olympic gold shooting with his other hand
623.place: London, United Kingdom, and Helsinki, Finland
623.event: In 1938 Hungarian army sergeant Karoly Takacs, a world-class pistol shooter, had his right shooting hand shattered when a faulty grenade exploded during army training. He taught himself to shoot with his left hand, won the Hungarian national pistol championship in 1939, and at the 1948 London Olympics won the rapid-fire pistol gold medal with a world record score. Four years later at Helsinki he won the event again, becoming its first repeat Olympic champion.
623.explanation: Takacs refused to let a career-ending injury end his career, and his comeback is still cited by the Olympic movement as one of its great stories of resilience.
623.tie_back: The kural says those who do not let sorrow grieve them bring grief upon sorrow itself, and Takacs turned the accident that should have finished him into the beginning of two Olympic victories.
623._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the kural's reversal, in which the misfortune rather than the man ends up defeated.

624.event_title: The Overland Telegraph is pushed through Australia's wet season
624.event: In 1870 South Australia began building a telegraph line of about 3,200 kilometres (some 2,000 miles) from Port Augusta to Darwin under Superintendent of Telegraphs Charles Todd. In the northern section the tropical wet season flooded creeks, halted the work teams and put the project months behind schedule, and Todd travelled north himself in early 1872 to push the work on. The line, with some 36,000 poles, was completed on 22 August 1872 and was soon linked to the undersea cable from Java, cutting communication time with Europe from months to hours.
624.explanation: Despite floods, spoiled supplies and a collapsed contract, the builders kept hauling the line forward, and Australia's isolation from the rest of the world ended.
624.tie_back: The kural pictures an ox that drags the cart through every rut and mire until the trouble itself suffers, and the telegraph builders kept dragging their line through every flooded creek until the obstacles gave way.
624._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of persistence through repeated physical obstacles; sources differ slightly on how many months late the northern section was.

625.event_title: Humayun loses his empire and regains Delhi years later
625.event: The Mughal emperor Humayun was defeated by Sher Shah Sur at Chausa in 1539 and at Kannauj in 1540 and was driven out of India. He took refuge with Shah Tahmasp of Persia, who gave him military aid, and he then took Kandahar and had to seize Kabul three times from his own disloyal brother Kamran. In 1555 he defeated Sikandar Sur at Sirhind and reoccupied Delhi and Agra, regaining his throne after more than a decade, though he died in an accident the following January.
625.explanation: Humayun suffered defeat, exile and betrayal by his own family one after another, yet he kept going and restored the Mughal dynasty that his son Akbar would make great.
625.tie_back: The kural says that even when troubles come piled one on another, the person who does not break inside makes those troubles suffer, and Humayun's long string of calamities ended in the recovery of his kingdom.
625._accuracy_note: A clear case of unbroken persistence through stacked misfortunes, though the sources document his actions rather than his inner state.

626.event_title: Chuck Feeney gives away his fortune and lives modestly
626.event: In 1984 Chuck Feeney, co-founder of the airport retailer Duty Free Shoppers, secretly transferred his entire 38.75 per cent stake in the company to his foundation, later known as The Atlantic Philanthropies, leaving himself with only a few million dollars. For the rest of his life he lived modestly in rented apartments, owned no car and flew economy. By the time the foundation closed in 2016 it had given away more than eight billion dollars.
626.explanation: Feeney treated his wealth as something to give rather than to hold, and he lived without the possessions that usually define a billionaire.
626.tie_back: The kural asks whether those who never clung to their wealth would ever wail at losing it, and Feeney, who chose to part with almost everything he owned, shows the detachment the couplet praises.
626._accuracy_note: Next-best only: Feeney shows the detachment the kural praises, but he gave his wealth away rather than losing it, so the couplet's scene of misfortune is not directly shown.

627.event_title: Matisse turns to paper cut-outs after major surgery
627.event: In 1941 Henri Matisse underwent serious abdominal surgery that left him in poor health and bedridden much of the time, often working from a bed or a wheelchair. Unable to stand at an easel for long, he turned increasingly to cutting shapes with scissors from paper painted with gouache by his assistants, which were then pinned up as he directed. These cut-outs, made in what he called a second life, became some of the most celebrated works of his career.
627.explanation: Matisse did not let a failing body become the end of his art; he treated its limits as a condition to work within and found a new form of expression.
627.tie_back: The kural says the noble know the body is simply a target for pain and so do not treat its distress as a true calamity, and Matisse, confined to bed and chair, went on creating as if his body's suffering were no disaster to his work.
627._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of not letting bodily affliction become a calamity of the spirit, though the sources describe his work rather than his inner attitude to pain.

628.event_title: The Zen poet Ryokan chooses a life of poverty in a mountain hut
628.event: Ryokan (1758-1831), a village headman's son who became a Zen Buddhist priest, never took charge of a temple. After years as a wandering mendicant he returned to his native Echigo province, where he lived mostly as a hermit in a small mountain hut, begging for alms. He is remembered as one of the great poets and calligraphers of the Edo period, and he often wrote with twigs or practised brushstrokes in the air when he could not afford brushes or paper.
628.explanation: Ryokan accepted hunger, cold and poverty as the ordinary conditions of his chosen life, and his poetry and calligraphy came out of that simplicity rather than in spite of it.
628.tie_back: The kural says one who does not chase pleasure and accepts hardship as natural never falls into real misery, and Ryokan, who sought no comfort and lived on alms, is remembered for serenity rather than suffering.
628._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of renouncing pleasure and accepting hardship as natural, though the details of his inner life come largely from his own poems.

629.event_title: Su Shi remains cheerful through exile to Huangzhou and Hainan
629.event: Su Shi, one of China's greatest poets and a successful official, was banished in 1079 to Huangzhou because of his opposition to the reforms of the minister Wang Anshi. There he farmed a plot on an eastern slope, took from it the name Dongpo, by which he is still known, and wrote some of his best-known works, including the Red Cliff rhapsodies of 1082. He showed the same optimism and lack of bitterness when he was banished again to Hainan Island in 1094, and he stayed on friendly terms with Wang Anshi, exchanging poems with him.
629.explanation: Su Shi's equanimity under disgrace became part of his fame, and the works he wrote in exile are among the best loved in Chinese literature.
629.tie_back: The kural says the one who does not greedily revel in good times will not be sunk in sorrow in bad times, and Su Shi, who moved from high office to a farmer's life without bitterness, shows the evenness of mind the couplet describes.
629._accuracy_note: Sources strongly document his calm in adversity; his restraint during prosperity, the couplet's other half, is less directly documented.

630.event_title: Abdelkader, after defeat and captivity, wins the esteem of Europe
630.event: Abdelkader, who led Algerian resistance against French conquest, surrendered in December 1847 on the promise of passage to the East but was instead held in France for about four years until Louis-Napoleon allowed his release in 1852. He settled in Damascus, and during the communal violence of July 1860 he and his followers sheltered and protected thousands of Christians at great personal risk. As a result he was highly commended by several European governments.
630.explanation: A defeated enemy who had endured years of broken promises and captivity emerged with a moral standing that the European powers themselves honoured.
630.tie_back: The kural says one who can take hardship as though it were sweet will win a distinction even enemies admire, and Abdelkader, after defeat and captivity, won praise from the very European world whose armies he had fought.
630._accuracy_note: A reasonable illustration of distinction admired by former foes, but the sources document his conduct rather than his attitude to hardship, and the praise came for his rescue work more than his endurance.
